Debut director Hiromasa Yonebayashi (When Marnie Was There, 2014) and Studio Ghibli teamed up for this film version of Mary Norton’s 1952 children’s classic The Borrowers, full of gorgeous imagery of the natural world. Arrietty is the daughter of a family of Borrowers—miniature people secretly living in an occupied house—who risk their home when she befriends a human boy.

item.title: To Catch a Thief in 4K — Aug 26
item.description:
Wednesday, August 26, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 46m
1955 | 106 min. | USA | Color | English | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Alfred Hitchcock WRITTEN BY: John Michael Hayes WITH: Cary Grant, Grace Kelly, Jesse Royce Landis, John Williams
Type: Screenings
John Robie (Cary Grant), a former French Resistance fighter and cat burglar, is enjoying his early retirement in the Riviera when a series of thefts make him once more the prime suspect—and for the beautiful heiress Frances Stevens (Grace Kelly), these suspicions only add to his appeal. Alfred Hitchcock paired two of Hollywood’s most effortlessly glamorous stars for this witty combination of romantic comedy and caper thriller, adapted by John Michael Hayes (Rear Window, 1954) from the novel by David Dodge. The Oscar-winning VistaVision cinematography of Hitchcock’s regular collaborator Robert Burks (Strangers on a Train, 1951) captures the beauty of the co-stars and the setting in all its splendor.

item.title: We’re No Angels in VistaVision — Aug 27
item.description:
Thursday, August 27, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 45m
1955 | 105 min. | USA | Technicolor | English | Not Rated | VistaVision DIRECTED BY: Michael Curtiz WRITTEN BY: Ranald MacDougall WITH: Humphrey Bogart, Aldo Ray, Peter Ustinov, Joan Bennett
Type: Screenings
“It isn’t fair! Here we are, three desperate criminals who will stop at nothing to escape from Devil’s Island, and we have to fall in with nice people!” So laments Jules (Peter Ustinov), one of a trio of convicts stuck on the French-controlled isle on Christmas Eve, 1895, where they fall in with the lovely proprietors of a local supply shop. Crime, romance, and dark comedy collide in an entertaining tale of unexpected guardian angels from director and star of Casablanca (1942) Michael Curtiz and Humphrey Bogart, with the actor in a rare comedic role. The material was rich enough for director Neil Jordan to revisit in 1989, this time with Oscar-winning stars Robert De Niro and Sean Penn.

item.title: North by Northwest in 70mm — Aug 28
item.description:
Friday, August 28, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 16m
1959 | 136 min. | USA | Color | English | 70mm DIRECTED BY: Alfred Hitchcock WRITTEN BY: Ernest Lehman WITH: Cary Grant, Eva Marie Saint, James Mason, Jessie Royce Landis
Type: Screenings
Hitchcock plays with the concept of the wrong man, a frequent theme in his narratives, in one of the most admired and entertaining of his mid-career films. North by Northwest stars four-time collaborator Grant as Roger O. Thornhill, a suave ad executive whose identity is mistaken for a government agent. Ruthless spy Philip Vandamm (James Mason) is after Thornhill; on a separate mission is a group of secret agents who follows Thornhill across the country. On the run, Thornhill meets Eve Kendall, a mesmerizing, peculiar woman whose mysterious identity amplifies the level of danger he is in. The film’s ironically ecstatic tone parallels the enchanting aspect of Grant’s portrayal of Thornhill—elegantly sarcastic with a witty sense of humor. Processed in Technicolor, this spectacular thriller showcases now-iconic action sequences such as the crop duster plane chase and climax at Mount Rushmore.

item.description:
Accessible screening

2016 | 108 min. | USA | Color | Scope | English | Open Captions | Rated PG | DCP DIRECTED BY: Byron Howard, Rich Moore WRITTEN BY: Jared Bush, Phil Johnston STORY BY: Byron Howard, Rich Moore, Jared Bush, Jim Reardon, Josie Trinidad, Phil Johnston, Jennifer Lee WITH: Ginnifer Goodwin, Jason Bateman, Idris Elba, Jenny Slate
Type: Screenings
Accessible screeningOn the last Saturday of every month, the museum's Family Matinee is an accommodative screening where we offer open captioning, keep the theater dimly lit, and maintain a lower volume specifically for neurodivergent viewers. When a young rabbit from Bunnyburrow moves to the big city of Zootopia to achieve her lifelong dream of becoming a police officer, she uncovers a sinister conspiracy. She also develops an unexpected friendship with a wily fox in this computer-animated comedy that imaginatively depicts a metropolis populated by animals of every type. The winner of the 2016 Animated Feature Film Oscar, Zootopia benefits from its expert voice cast, led by Ginnifer Goodwin as the bunny cop, Jason Bateman as the cynical fox, and Idris Elba as the world-weary Cape buffalo police chief.

item.title: The Court Jester in 4K — Aug 29
item.description:
Saturday, August 29, 2026 at 2 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 41m
1956 | 101 min. | USA | Technicolor | English | Not Rated | 4K DCP DIRECTED/ WRITTEN BY: Norman Panama, Melvin Frank WITH: Danny Kaye, Glynis Johns, Basil Rathbone, Angela Lansbury
Type: Screenings
The second film from Dena Enterprises, the production company founded by actor Danny Kaye (White Christmas, 1954) and his songwriter wife, Sylvia Fine, The Court Jester is a delightful vehicle for the comedic icon to showcase his unparalleled timing, physical humor, and witty wordplay. Kaye is Hubert Hawkins, a retired carnival performer who disguises himself as a jester to help overturn an evil plot against a rightful British king. This ridiculous romp, with undeniable star Kaye at its center, is buttressed by a sincere Glynis Johns (Mary Poppins, 1964) as Maid Jean and an arch Basil Rathbone (Sherlock Holmes,1939–1946) as Lord Ravenhurst. The most expensive comedy ever made at the time, primarily for its lavish sets, The Court Jester earned Kaye a Golden Globe nomination, and in 2004, the National Film Registry added the film to its list of titles considered “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.”

item.description:

1957 | 126 min. | USA | Black-and-White | English | Not Rated | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Charles Vidor WRITTEN BY: Oscar Saul WITH: Frank Sinatra, Mitzi Gaynor, Jeanne Crain, Eddie Albert
Type: Screenings
This gritty biopic dives into the smoky, dangerous glamor of Prohibition-era Chicago for the true story of nightclub performer Joe E. Lewis, famous for being one of the few people who could make gangster Al Capone laugh. Crooner Frank Sinatra, lauded by the film's marketing as “the most electric personality of our time,” follows Lewis’s highs and lows with the same realism and range he brought to The Man with the Golden Arm (1955). Ol’ Blue Eyes also adds musical dimension to the character — the real Lewis was more comedian than singer—with director Charles Vidor (no relation to fellow director King) compounding his experience with musicals and comedies into a story with dramatic nuance.

item.title: Artists and Models in 4K — Aug 30
item.description:

1956 | 109 min. | USA | Color | English | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Frank Tashlin WRITTEN BY: Frank Tashlin, Hal Kanter, Herbert Baker ADAPTATION BY: Don McGuire WITH: Dean Martin, Jerry Lewis, Shirley MacLaine, Dorothy Malone
Type: Screenings
This zany romantic comedy was the fourteenth film to pair iconic comic duo Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis, released a year before their professional breakup. Martin plays Rick, a struggling painter, and Lewis is his roommate, Eugene, who is obsessed with a comic book character called Bat Lady. They become entangled with Bat Lady’s creator (Dorothy Malone) and her roommate/model (Shirley MacLaine) in a farcical plot that manages to incorporate government secrets and enemy spies. Frank Tashlin’s background in animation made him the perfect choice to direct this cartoon-infused romp, and he would collaborate often with Lewis after the split with Martin.

item.title: Da 5 Bloods — Aug 30
item.description:
Sunday, August 30, 2026 at 2 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 36m
2020 | 156 min. | USA | Color | Scope | English, Vietnamese | Rated R | DCP DIRECTED BY: Spike Lee WRITTEN BY: Danny Bilson, Paul Demeo, Kevin Wilmott, Spike Lee WITH: Delroy Lindo, Jonathan Majors, Clarke Peters, Norm Lewis
Type: Screenings
Four veterans return to the jungles of Vietnam in hopes of recovering a buried fortune in director/co-writer Spike Lee’s epic adventure drama, which pays homage to the classic The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (a favorite of the filmmaker’s) while exploring the rarely told experiences of Black soldiers in the Vietnam War. The top-notch cast includes Sinners supporting actor nominee Delroy Lindo as a proud Trump supporter; two stars of TV’s The Wire, Clarke Peters and Isiah Whitlock, Jr.; and Chadwick Boseman in one of his final performances. The film’s one Oscar nomination was earned by seven-time Grammy winner Terence Blanchard, a regular collaborator of Lee’s, whose bold orchestral score sits comfortably alongside the vintage Marvin Gaye songs that fill the film’s soundtrack.

item.title: The Girl Rush in 4K — Aug 30
item.description:
Sunday, August 30, 2026 at 3 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 25m
1955 | 85 min. | USA | Technicolor | English | Not Rated | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Robert Pirosh WRITTEN BY: Robert Pirosh, Jerome Davis WITH: Rosalind Russell, Fernando Lamas, Eddie Albert, Gloria DeHaven
Type: Screenings
Fast-talking Rosalind Russell (His Girl Friday, 1940) is absolutely captivating as Kim Halliday, the daughter of a deceased career gambler who joins her father’s former business partner to run a Vegas casino. Russell's unflappable confidence is a fine match for the swagger of Fernando Lamas as Victor Monte, a rival club owner who vies for Kim’s affections—and her casino. There’s nothing quite like the neon lights of Sin City captured in high-definition VistaVision and vibrant Technicolor, which appear here in gorgeous documentary footage of the Strip; like most studio productions of the era, however, the bulk of this musical comedy was shot on producer Paramount’s lot.

item.title: One Battle After Another in VistaVision — Aug 30
item.description:
In person: director Paul Thomas Anderson, cinematographer Michael Bauman, and producer Sara Murphy
Sunday, August 30, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 42m
2025 | 162 min. | USA | Color | English/Spanish | Rated R | VistaVision DIRECTED/WRITTEN BY: Paul Thomas Anderson WITH: Leonardo Di Caprio, Sean Penn, Benicio Del Toro, Teyana Taylor
Type: Screenings
Paul Thomas Anderson won Oscars for Directing, Adapted Screenplay and Best Picture (along with fellow producers Adam Somner and Sara Murphy) for his epic comedy-thriller, loosely based on Thomas Pynchon’s 1990 novel Vineland, about a retired revolutionary (Best Actor nominee Leonardo DiCaprio) trying to protect his teenage daughter from a fanatical military officer (Supporting Actor winner Sean Penn). Anderson’s longtime casting director Cassandra Kulukundis won the Academy’s inaugural Oscar for Casting, her expertly chosen ensemble including past Oscar winners (including Supporting Actor nominee Benicio Del Toro), veteran character actors, comedy writers, and impressive newcomers such as Chase Infiniti, who plays DiCaprio’s daughter. Anderson appears for a Q&A before the screening, along with cinematographer Michael Bauman, and producer Sara Murphy.

1961 | 141 min. | USA | Color | English, Spanish | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Marlon Brando WRITTEN BY: Guy Trosper, Calder Willingham WITH: Marlon Brando, Karl Malden, Katy Jurado, Pina Pellicer
Type: Screenings
Marlon Brando took on his only feature directing project—following the last-minute departure of original director Stanley Kubrick—with this character-oriented Western about a bank robber who tracks down a friend (frequent Brando co-star Karl Malden) who betrayed him. The Academy Award–nominated VistaVision color cinematography by Charles Lang Jr. (How the West Was Won,1962) makes strong use of scenic locations in Mexico and California, with vivid imagery of Brando riding his horse along the Monterey coastline. Until 2024, One-Eyed Jacks was the final film shot with the VistaVision process.

item.title: Monkey Business in 4K — Sep 2
item.description:
Wednesday, September 2, 2026 at 2:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 37m
1952 | 97 min | USA | Black-and-White | English | Not Rated | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Howard Hawks PRODUCED BY: Sol C. Siegel WRITTEN BY: Ben Hecht, Charles Lederer, I. A. L. Diamond WITH: Cary Grant, Ginger Rogers, Charles Coburn, Marilyn Monroe
Type: Screenings
Dr. Barnaby Fulton (Cary Grant) is a scatterbrained chemist working to create an elixir of youth. When one of his chimpanzees, Esther, breaks loose, she mixes chemicals in Barnaby’s lab, dumping the concoction into the office’s water cooler. The formula generates the rejuvenation effect Barnaby has been seeking — along with more chaotic side effects in some cases. Monkey Business allowed Monroe, who co-stars as Lois Laurel, to showcase her brilliant timing, further solidifying her reputation as a comedic actress.

item.description:
In person: Academy Governor Patricia Dehaney Selected by the Makeup Artists and Hairstylists Branch
Wednesday, September 2, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures

1939 | 133 min. | USA | Black-and-white, color | English | DCP DIRECTED BY: George Cukor PRODUCED BY: Hunt Stromberg WRITTEN BY: Anita Loos, Jane Murfin WITH: Norma Shearer, Joan Crawford, Rosalind Russell, Mary Boland
Type: Screenings
Co-written by Anita Loos and Jane Murfin, The Women delivers 135 of them, each with a speaking role, to the exclusion of men. The delightfully witty and rapid-fire dialogue pours out of a cadre of familiar faces, including Norma Shearer, Joan Crawford, and Rosalind Russell. While most of the film unfolds in black-and-white, a delightful six-minute Technicolor fashion show is included, featuring gowns by Adrian, the iconic, MGM-based costume designer. Contributing to the distinctive looks of the cast was the uncredited hair designer, MGM veteran Sydney Guilaroff, whose film career spanned the 1930s to the 1980s and included such classics as Singin’ in the Rain (1952), North by Northwest (1959) and Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1966)

item.title: Barry Lyndon in 35mm — Sep 3
item.description:
Thursday, September 3, 2026 at 7 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 3h 5m
1975 | 185 min | UK, USA | Color | English | Rated PG | 35mm DIRECTED/WRITTEN/PRODUCED BY: Stanley Kubrick. WITH: Ryan O’Neal, Marisa Berenson, Patrick Magee, Hardy Kruger. New print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.
Type: Screenings
Stanley Kubrick’s follow-up to the foreboding A Clockwork Orange (1971) is a stately, gorgeously crafted, epic adaptation of William Makepeace Thackeray’s novel about the curious fates of an Irish rogue. Ryan O’Neal portrays Lyndon, and the film earned seven nominations, including Best Picture, Directing, and Adapted Screenplay (all for Kubrick), with Oscars going to the Art Direction, Costume Design, Adaptation Score, and John Alcott’s painterly, natural and candlelit cinematography, which remains immensely influential.

1996 | 120 min. | Australia/USA/Canada | Color | Scope | English | Rated PG-13 | 35mm DIRECTED BY: Baz Luhrmann WRITTEN BY: Craig Pearce, Baz Luhrmann PRODUCED BY: Gabriella Martinelli, Baz Luhrmann WITH: Leonardo DiCaprio, Claire Danes, Brian Dennehy, John Leguizamo
Type: Screenings
Baz Luhrmann’s take on Shakespeare’s tragedy is perhaps one of the best-loved adaptations and is the second installment in his Red Curtain Trilogy, which closed with Moulin Rouge! (2001). Featuring Luhrmann’s distinctive, stylized palate coupled with frenetic, MTV-style editing and an all-star soundtrack, Romeo + Juliet became a classic for its casting, with Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes playing the star-crossed lovers. Print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.

item.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs — Sep 5
item.description:
Saturday, September 5, 2026 at 11 am
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 23m
1937 | 83 min. | USA | Color | English | Rated G | DCP DIRECTED BY: David Hand, Perce Pearce, William Cottrell, Larry Morey, Wilfred Jackson, Ben Sharpsteen PRODUCED BY: Walt Disney WRITTEN BY: Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank, Webb Smith WITH: Adriana Caselotti, Harry Stockwell, Lucille La Verne, Moroni Olsen
Type: Screenings
Snow White, orphaned as a child, is forced to work under the reign of her evil stepmother, the Queen, who will stop at nothing to remain the most beautiful being in the land. When Snow White’s beauty grows, so does the Queen’s jealously. Seething with hatred, the Queen concocts a sinister plan to put an end to her. Will the princess escape her fate and achieve her happily ever after? Based on the classic Brothers Grimm fairy tale, this first animated feature from The Walt Disney Company—and the first traditionally animated feature ever produced— was nominated for its original score; the following year, the Academy gave Disney a Special Award for the film (one full-sized Oscar and seven small ones), “recognized as a significant screen innovation which has charmed millions and pioneered a great new entertainment field for the motion picture cartoon.”

item.title: Fanny & Alexander in 35mm — Sep 5
item.description:
Saturday, September 5, 2026 at 2:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 3h 8m
1982 | 188 min. | Sweden/France/West Germany | Color | Swedish/German/Yiddish with English subtitles | Rated R | 35mm DIRECTED/WRITTEN BY: Ingmar Bergman PRODUCED BY: Jörn Donner WITH: Kristina Adolphson, Börje Ahlstedt, Bertil Guve, Pernilla Allwin
Type: Screenings
Swedish auteur Ingmar Bergman’s most sentimental and autobiographical work is set in turn-of-the-century Sweden and appropriately bathed in the candlelit interiors common of the era. Unfolding through the eyes of 10-year-old Alexander, a boy from a wealthy family that operates the town theater, the narrative spans seasons and holidays, marriages and deaths, with small moments of daily life punctuating childhood milestones. Originally conceived as a television miniseries of more than five hours, the final, 188-minute version allowed the visuals of two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Sven Nykvist (Fanny & Alexander was one of his wins) to be admired at a scale befitting this epic drama. New print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.

item.title: Top Hat in 35mm — Sep 6
item.description:
Sunday, September 6, 2026 at 2 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 40m
1935 | 100 min. | USA | Black-and-White | English | 35mm DIRECTED BY: Mark Sandrich WRITTEN BY: Dwight Taylor, Allan Scott STORY BY: Dwight Taylor PRODUCED BY: Pandro S. Berman WITH: Fred Astaire, Ginger Rogers, Edward Everett Horton, Erik Rhodes
Type: Screenings
An American tap dancer pursues the woman he loves from London to Venice in the fourth movie musical to feature the iconic team of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, and the second of their films to receive a Best Picture nomination, following The Gay Divorcee (1934). Spotlighting the stars at their effortless best, it was also nominated for Irving Berlin’s classic “Cheek to Cheek,” Hermes Pan’s dance direction of the numbers “Piccolino” and “Top Hat, White Tie, and Tails,” and the art direction of Van Nest Polglase and Carroll Clark, whose elegant deco sets include a Venice canal constructed on a Los Angeles soundstage. New print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.

item.title: Amadeus in 4K — Sep 6
item.description:
Sunday, September 6, 2026 at 6 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 38m
1984 | 158 min | USA | Color | Scope | English | Rated PG | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Miloš Forman PRODUCED BY: Saul Zaentz WRITTEN BY: Peter Shaffer WITH: F. Murray Abraham, Tom Hulce, Elizabeth Berridge, Simon Callow Original theatrical release version 4k restoration by The Academy Film Archive and The Saul Zaentz Co. with restoration funding provided by Teatro Della Pace Films.
Type: Screenings
Miloš Forman directed Peter Shaffer’s screenplay, based on his Tony Award–winning play, about the 18th century rivalry between journeyman court composer Antonio Salieri (F. Murray Abraham in an Academy Award–winning tour de force) and young upstart Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (fellow Best Actor nominee Tom Hulce). Saul Zaentz’s lavish production features opulent period details, while Shaffer’s witty script speaks eloquently about the challenge of art while leaving room for Mozart’s gorgeous music. The film earned 11 nominations, and its eight Oscar wins include Best Picture, Art Direction, Costume Design, Directing, Makeup, Sound, and for Shaffer’s adapted screenplay.

item.title: Niagara — Sep 7
item.description:
Monday, September 7, 2026 at 2:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 32m
1953 | 92 min | USA | Technicolor | English | Not Rated | DCP DIRECTED BY: Henry Hathaway PRODUCED BY: Charles Brackett WRITTEN BY: Charles Brackett, Walter Reisch, Richard Breen WITH: Marilyn Monroe, Joseph Cotten, Jean Peters, Casey Adams
Type: Screenings
Newlyweds Ray and Polly Cutler (Jean Peters and Casey Adams) take a postponed honeymoon at Niagara Falls, where they encounter Rose and George Loomis (Marilyn Monroe and Joseph Cotten). The Loomis’s rocky relationship hangs over the couple’s romantic getaway, further complicated by a murder. 1953 was an important year for Monroe with the successes of Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and How to Marry a Millionaire in the following months, and her breakout performance as the sensual Rose in Niagara catapulted the actor into superstardom.

item.description:
Selected by the Marketing and Public Relations Branch

1994 | 104 min. | Australia | Color | Scope | English | Rated R | 35mm DIRECTED/WRITTEN BY: Stephan Elliott PRODUCED BY: Al Clark, Michael Hamlyn WITH: Terence Stamp, Hugo Weaving, Guy Pearce, Bill Hunter
Type: Screenings
Two drag queens and a transgender woman drive across the Australian outback in a tour bus named Priscilla, in this wild road comedy that earned Lizzy Gardiner and Tim Chappell Oscars for their imaginative costume designs. Terence Stamp gives an impressive change-of-pace performance as the world-weary Bernadette, and he’s matched by Hugo Weaving as the trio’s conflicted leader. Guy Pearce delivers a breakout performance as the youngest of the group. Deftly mixing campy humor and genuine emotion amidst stunning locations, Priscilla was an international success and spawned a hit stage musical. Print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.

Type: Screenings
A student from a Virginian girl's school during the American Civil War discovers a Union Army corporal wounded in the woods and takes him in. Attracted to the handsome enemy soldier, the women of the home allow him to stay. This intense gothic thriller is filled with jealousy, rage, and betrayals. Based on the 1966 novel by Thomas P. Cullinan, this adaptation stars Colin Farrell, Nicole Kidman, Elle Fanning, and Kirsten Dunst. The Beguiled earned director Sofia Coppola the Prix de la mise en scene (Best Director Award) at the 2017 Cannes Film Festival.

Internationally renowned fine artist Tacita Dean presents her rarely screened The Uncles (2004), in which the sons of Ealing Studios icons Basil Dean and Sir Michael Balcon reflect on their fathers’ careers and personal lives in an extended conversation with historian and curator Laurence Kardish. Filmed and projected in anamorphic 16mm, The Uncles offers an unusual widescreen portrait of two loquacious, charming English gentlemen (Winton Dean and Jonathan Balcon) illuminating the accomplishments, failings, and elusive humanity of their eminent fathers with wit, candor, and understated complexity. Beyond the copious anecdotal nuggets of interest to any fan of classic British cinema, the film also grants intimate access to two men who both admired and struggled to truly know their fathers as they consider their own youths in pre-war Britain. In conjunction with this screening and organized by Los Angeles’ Marciano Art Foundation (MAF) director Hanneke Skerath and Mark Toscano, MAF will present the US debut of Dean’s landmark installation, FILM (2011), from September 18, 2026, through January 2, 2027. On Halloween night, 1963, in the small Illinois town of Haddonfield, 6-year-old Michael Myers commits a horribly violent act against his older sister. Type: Screenings
The second feature from director-choreographer Bob Fosse is one of his greatest works in any medium. It’s a dazzling adaptation of the John Kander-Fred Ebb Broadway show, inspired by Christopher Isherwood’s The Berlin Stories, and a fine demonstration of how a movie musical rooted in realism can be as satisfying as the more traditional variety. When naïve young Brian Roberts (Michael York as the Isherwood figure) moves into a Berlin boardinghouse in 1931, he is unprepared for his new neighbor—the brash, would-be star Sally Bowles, played by Liza Minnelli in her Oscar-winning, career-defining performance. The film received 10 nominations (including Best Picture) and won eight Oscars, including for Fosse’s direction, Joel Grey’s supporting performance, and the art direction of Rolf Zehetbauer, Jurgen Kiebach and set decorator Herbert Strabel. Their work brought the film’s time and place to life and provided Fosse with a realistically claustrophobic Kit Kat Klub, which nonetheless made room for the filmmaker’s typically thrilling musical numbers.

In October 1995, group of African American men board a bus for a cross-country trip to Washington D.C. They have different backgrounds and hold varying beliefs, but they’re all on the way to the same march. Among them are a father and a teenage son forced together by court order; a gay couple on the verge of a breakup; an aspiring actor who’s homophobic and loud about it; and a man whose father, a police officer, was killed, he says, “by a brother.” Most of the film takes place in or around the moving bus as the conversations grow more personal, and emotions roil to the surface. Spike Lee’s Get on the Bus, which was shot in three weeks, was financed by a small group of men including Danny Glover, Wesley Snipes, Will Smith, and Johnnie Cochran. Inspired by the Million Man March of 1995, Lee's film delves into the racism that has influenced Black communities for generations, creating space for genuine, and difficult, discourse about the community’s inner and outward-facing conflicts.

In Ray’s remarkable debut feature, classic noir elements blend effortlessly with melodrama to create something entirely new, making They Live by Night a standout of the period, realized with lived-in dialogue beautifully adapted from Edward Anderson’s source material and shot primarily on location in greater Los Angeles. The film is notable too for its innovative camera techniques and tracking shots, especially in the driving sequences. This warm-up for Rebel Without a Cause (1955) finds Ray arriving on the scene fully formed with a confident and inimitable style. A favorite of cartoonist Nathan Gelgud and critic A. S. Murnau’s visionary 1926 silent adaptation, a masterpiece of haunting visual design that explores rich themes of morality and materialism. Starring Oscar-winning actor Emil Jannings as the terrifying trickster Mephisto, Murnau’s tale emerges from the disturbing underworld into the dreams of lost innocence for one of the most remarkable films from the German Expressionist milieu. A century later, scores of international filmmakers, including Guillermo del Toro, Jennifer Kent, and Robert Eggers, continue to be influenced by this masterwork. The Academy Museum is thrilled to present this film with live accompaniment on the occasion of its centennial and of MUBI’s newest publication, The Faust Bible: The Making of F. W. Made for less than $20,000 just after the liberation of Italy by US forces, Rossellini’s first installment in his Neo-Realist Trilogy, which also includes Paisan (1946, screening on November 15) and Germany, Year Zero (1948, screening the same day), is also considered the first product of neo-realism. The devastation of Nazi-occupied Rome serves as an all-too-real backdrop for a story that could have been ripped from the headlines: a resistance leader (Aldo Fabrizi) is pursued through town as he seeks shelter and a safe escape. With “the terror of German occupation [...] still vivid in the minds of everyone,” (Patrizio Rossi, 1988) including Rossellini’s lead actress, the great Anna Magnani, Rome, Open City serves as a prototype for a series of films that characterize the best of Italian cinema.

Sugarcoated Arsenic 2013 | 20 min | USA | Black-and-white | Sound | Not Rated | DCP Pride 2021 | 7 min | USA | Color | Sound | Not Rated | DCP Accidental Athlete 2023 | 7 min | USA | Black-and-white | Sound | Not Rated | DCP 70kg 2017 | 2 min | USA | Black-and-white | Silent | Not Rated | DCP How Can I Ever Be Late 2017 | 5 min | USA | Black-and-white | Sound | Not Rated | DCP Gospel Hill 2022 | 5 min | USA | Black-and-white | Sound | Not Rated | DCP Black Bus Stop 2019 | 9 min | USA | Color | Sound | Not Rated | DCP Total program runtime: approx. 57 min

Since 2013, artist Kevin Jerome Everson and author and historian Claudrena N. Harold have cooperated on a series of lyrical short films—13 to date—that explore Black intellectual, social, and political life at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, where both are professors. Collectively titled Black Fire, these works highlight the spaces where Black students have studied, learned, and organized through the years, including the school's student-run newspaper and a bus stop that became a locus for collective action. Through short films spotlighting figures such as Paulette Jones Morant, one of the first Black woman scholastic athletes at UVA, and Vivian Gordon, the director of UVA’s Black Studies program from 1974–1980, Black Fire creates significant space for otherwise under-the-radar figures. Employing interviews and reenactment, often casting their students as performers, Everson and Harold's films bring the history of UVA, as well as the historical experiences of Black students and faculty across the US, into meaningful conversation with the present day.
Filmmakers Kevin Jerome Everson and Claudrena N. Harold appear in conversation after the films, moderated by filmmaker Cauleen Smith.

The second installment in his WWII trilogy and one of Rossellini’s favorites of his films, the episodic Paisàn is another depiction of the tribulations of the Italians under German occupation. Released the same year the first theories of neo-realism were published in film magazines Esprit, La Revue du Cinéma, and Bianco e Nero by acclaimed critics, including André Bazin, Germany Year Zero rounds out Rossellini’s WWII trilogy and brings a continental scope to the devastating impact of Hitler’s final solution. By centering the story on a young boy navigating the devastating implications of war, Rossellini accentuates the stark contrast between generations. A major influence on François Truffaut’s The 400 Blows (1959) and cast with people the director found by exploring the four zones of Berlin, Germany Year Zero would, Rossellini hoped, “reproduce the truth exactly as the camera saw it for that audience through the entire world which has a heart capable of love and a brain capable of thought.”

Named for the volcanic island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, Rossellini's first collaboration with Swedish actress Ingrid Bergman is a heartbreaking tale about a young Baltic woman who follows an Italian fisherman to his tiny, isolated village. Married swiftly after their release from an internment camp, she begins to struggle as her refined upbringing clashes with the rough local lifestyle, causing strain on her marriage and her psyche. It was Bergman who first contacted Rossellini after seeing Paisàn in 1948 in hopes of collaborating, and the making of Stromboli marks the beginning of a love affair that ended the filmmaker’s marriage and caused an international scandal when Bergman announced their pregnancy. For Rossellini, the project also signals a creative shift, at least to some critics, away from realism and into a deeply psychological phase.

Inspired by the writings of Saint Francis of Assisi and the hagiographic texts about his loyal follower Brother Juniper, The Flowers of St. Francis is composed of simple vignettes that beautifully illustrate the humane life lessons of the People’s Saint. One of Roberto Rossellini's most singular and unheralded works, this potent blend of neorealism and fantasy is an idiosyncratic, lighthearted fable. In a fishing village on the Amalfi Coast, a stranger claiming to be a saint bestows a photographer’s camera with the power to kill bad people by photographing existing pictures of them. Initially, the photographer uses his newfound weapon to eliminate abusers of power. But before long, he succumbs to the very same amoral selfishness he once claimed to despise. Type: Screenings
According to Roberto Rossellini, Europe ’51 is a retelling of his film The Flowers of St. Francis (Francesco, giullare di Dio, 1950), from a female perspective. Ingrid Bergman portrays a wealthy American socialite living in Rome, moving through grief and guilt over the death of her son. As she sets out on a journey of newfound selflessness, devoting her time and money to the less fortunate, her husband and the community question her sanity. With Rossellini often pushing his actors to improvise dialogue, Ingrid would receive her lines only minutes before rolling. She would often reference this time as a difficult challenge. Working with first-time actors, with no written dialogue, and all during a Roman heat wave while Ingrid was pregnant with twins Isabella and Isotta, the director and actress proved their grit as a filmmaking duo.

In this filmed version of Paul Claudel and Arthur Honegger’s oratorio, or sung mystery play, Rossellini’s wife, Ingrid Bergman, plays Saint Joan of Arc in the final minutes of her life. In a 1954 interview, Rossellini said of the project: “It’s a very strange film. I know it will be said that my involution has reached its maximum limit, that I am digging my own grave.
